title: Rawalpindi, March 1947
hookLine: months before Partition, Sikh villages near Rawalpindi were attacked, and women took their own lives rather than be taken

lines: A WELL IN A VILLAGE COURTYARD.
cards: A well in the courtyard of a village gurdwara, in the hills near Rawalpindi, in what is now Pakistan. In March of 1947, months before the border was drawn, armed mobs attacked Sikh and Hindu villages across that district.
Houses burned. People were killed. In the village of Thoa Khalsa, survivors later told a historian, a large group of the village's women went into the well rather than be taken by the attackers.
This lesson will not linger on how. It stays with the women, and with how they are remembered.

teach.h: THE KILLING STARTED BEFORE THE BORDER.
teach.b: First, before the border. Partition is often told as a story that began when the line was drawn. Rawalpindi is a reminder that the killing started earlier, while the politicians were still talking.
Second, the listener. The historian Urvashi Butalia sat with Partition survivors, recorded their memories, and wrote about Thoa Khalsa.

The families who survived remember those women as martyrs, shaheed, who chose death over capture and dishonor. Each year, she wrote, the story was retold to the community. Third, a harder question, asked gently.

teach.h: HOW MUCH CHOICE DID THEY HAVE?
teach.b: Butalia also asked how much choice the women had, when fathers and brothers and the fear of capture stood around them. She didn't throw out the families' memory. She held it next to the question, and let both stand.
That's a kind of respect too: refusing to make anyone's death simpler than it was. Fourth, an older grief.

Tradition says Guru Nanak himself saw an invading army sweep across Punjab, and in a hymn kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 417, he mourned for women whose braided hair, once parted with vermilion, was shorn, and whose finery was taken.

The Guru's own words didn't look away from what war does to women. So this week, which ran from women marching in the reform years, through the trenches, the turbans, a second war and a thousand days, ends here at a well.
Not with an explanation. With a name, Thoa Khalsa, and a decision to remember.

how: Sikh families from the Rawalpindi villages and their descendants remember the women of March 1947 as martyrs, and the story is retold in the community and in histories of Partition.

games.q: you're a historian. the survivors tell you the women of the village chose martyrdom. what do you do?
o: set their memory aside as legend.
write down only their version, with no questions.
honor their memory, and also ask how much choice the women had.
games.why: Urvashi Butalia did both: she recorded the families' memory of martyrdom and gently asked how free the women's choice was, letting both stand.

practice: If this story is close to your own family's, go easy with yourself, and stop whenever you need to.
You don't need to picture anything: just hold the women of those villages in mind, without faces, without details, the way you'd hold someone's hand at a funeral, and let the silence do the rest.
If you pray, say Waheguru softly on the breath out.

wordCard.voice: Rawalpindi. The district in the hills where, months before Partition, Sikh and Hindu villages were attacked, and the women of Thoa Khalsa died rather than be taken. Today's word.
